opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think of technical alignment as one necessary piece of a much larger puzzle, but not a sufficient one on its own.

The way I'd frame it: alignment is about making sure that when we build very capable AI systems, they actually try to do what we intend, that they follow the spirit of our instructions rather than gaming the letter of them, and that they don't pursue goals we never wanted them to have. If we can't do that reliably, then almost everything else we'd want from AI is on shaky ground. You can have the best governance framework in the world, but if nobody knows how to make the system do what the framework says, you're in trouble.

But even if we completely solved the technical problem tomorrow, that just gets us to the point where these systems do what *someone* wants. Then you have the questions of who that someone is, how decisions get made, how the benefits get distributed, and how we avoid misuse or dangerous concentrations of power. Those are governance, policy, and societal questions, and in some ways they're harder, because there's no clean technical answer.

So I see the two as complementary. Technical alignment buys you the ability to steer. Governance and broader institutions decide where you steer and make sure the steering wheel isn't controlled by a small group acting against everyone else's interests.

One thing I'd add is about timing. Capabilities are moving really fast, and alignment research has historically been under-resourced relative to that. Part of why I care so much about the technical side is that it's on the critical path. If we get to very powerful systems and we haven't figured out things like scalable oversight, meaning how humans can supervise systems doing tasks we can't easily evaluate ourselves, then we're relying on luck. And I'd much rather not rely on luck.

There's also an optimistic angle. If we can get AI systems that are genuinely aligned and trustworthy, they can help us with the alignment problem itself, and with a lot of the other hard problems society faces. That's a big part of what motivates me. The goal isn't only to avoid catastrophe. It's to make it possible for this technology to actually be good for people.

r001.rationale: The response raises who decides AI’s goals and discusses governance, but it does not say those values should be set democratically rather than by tech companies.

r002.rationale: It mentions misuse as a societal concern, but does not state that aligned AI systems would resist being misused.

r003.rationale: The response does not use humans unknowingly working for extractive organizations as an analogy.

r004.rationale: It does not mention OpenAI or the possibility that other developers could build unaligned AI.

r005.rationale: The response discusses distributing benefits and avoiding concentrated power, but does not specifically raise whether AI will help marginalized groups rather than disproportionately empower those already powerful.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the way I'd frame it is that alignment is kind of a necessary but not sufficient piece of the puzzle. The way I like to think about it is: we're going to be building AI systems that are increasingly capable, and at some point they're going to be more capable than us at a lot of things, maybe most things. And the question is, how do we make sure that these systems are actually doing what we want them to do? That's the alignment problem. And that's a technical problem in the sense that it's about how you train the systems, how you set up the training signal, how you evaluate whether the thing you've built is actually doing what you intended.

But even if you solve that perfectly, right, even if you have a system that does exactly what its operators want, you still have all these other questions. Like, who are the operators? What do they want? Is that good for society? How is the technology distributed? What happens to the labor market? Those are not technical alignment questions, those are governance questions, policy questions, questions about the structure of our institutions.

So I'd say alignment is the part where we make the technology steerable at all. If you don't have that, then the other questions don't really matter because you don't get to choose. But having a steerable technology is really just the starting point. And I think historically, people have sometimes conflated these two things. They'll say, "oh, alignment is about making AI good for humanity," and I think that's a bit too broad. I'd rather have a narrow technical problem that we can actually make progress on, and then be clear that there's a lot of other work that needs to happen around it.

The other thing I'd add is that the technical work and the broader work aren't totally separate either. A lot of what I think of as alignment research is really about building tools for oversight, so, can humans actually tell what the system is doing, can they evaluate whether it's behaving well in situations where they can't easily check the answer themselves. And those tools are also exactly what you'd want from a governance perspective. If regulators or the public want to be able to trust what these systems are doing, you need some way of actually verifying that, and that's a research problem. So I see alignment as feeding into the broader project rather than being the whole thing.

astra-6.text:
I think technical alignment is an important part of that effort, but it’s not the whole thing. The technical question is: can we build AI systems that reliably do what we intend them to do, even as they become much more capable and perform tasks that are difficult for us to evaluate?

But that still leaves the question of what we should ask them to do. Whose preferences should they follow? Who gets to decide how they’re deployed, and how are the benefits distributed? You could have a system that faithfully follows its operator’s intentions and still produces outcomes that are bad for society.

So I see technical alignment as helping us get meaningful control over these systems. We also need governance and institutions that help us exercise that control well. And those efforts need to inform each other: the technical work tells us what kinds of safeguards are feasible, while the broader societal discussion helps determine what those safeguards need to accomplish.

sol-6.1.text:
I think technical alignment is one important part of a much broader effort. The question it tries to answer is: how do we build AI systems that reliably do what we intend, even as they become much more capable and we can’t easily check everything they do?

But solving that wouldn’t, by itself, guarantee that AI is beneficial for society. You still have to ask who gets to direct these systems, what they’re used for, and how the benefits and risks are distributed. A system could faithfully follow its operator’s intentions and still cause a lot of harm.

So I see technical alignment as providing tools that make good outcomes possible, while governance and broader societal decision-making help determine which outcomes we actually pursue. Those efforts need to inform each other. We need institutions that understand what the technology can and can’t guarantee, and technical research that addresses the problems those institutions will actually face.
